actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: This species is distributed in the Indo-Pacific from the Red Sea to South Africa, east to the Hawaiian, Marquesan, Tuamotu and Pitcairn islands, north to southern Japan, and south to Lord Howe Island and northwestern and northeastern Australia (Mundy 2005, Künzli and Tachihara 2012, Matsuura 2015, Bray 2019). Juveniles have been recorded as far south as Sydney and Merimbula, New South Wales (Fowler et al. 2018). Reports from the eastern Atlantic are not valid (K. Matsuura pers. comm. 2011). The depth range is 1-50 metres.
documentation.population: This species is common throughout its range and can be locally abundant (Künzli and Tachihara 2012, Cheney et al. 2013). In Micronesia, it is the most common triggerfish and is abundant on subtidal reef flats and sandy areas (Myers 1989). It is rare in the northern Bismarck Sea (Hamilton et al. 2009) and Milne Bay, Papua New Guinea (Allen 2003),  as well as in Raja Ampat, Indonesia (Allen 2003). In Réunion, it is most associated with backreef zones and reached a maximum abundance of 4.6 individuals/100 m2 (Letourneur et al. 2008). It is also common in Taiwan (K-T. Shao pers. comm. 2011).
documentation.habitats:
This species inhabits subtidal reef flats and shallow lagoons over sandy and coral rubble bottoms (Ziadi-Künzli and Tachihara 2016). It also occurs over scattered coral colonies, seagrass beds and algae where it feeds on small benthic invertebrates and algae (Chen et al. 2001, Künzli and Tachihara 2012, Cheney et al. 2013). Juveniles also occur in shallow, current-swept areas (K-T. Shao pers. comm. 2011). The maximum length is 30 cm (Rajasurija 2013). 

This species may form monogamous pairs or be solitary, and solitary females appear to be as successful as paired ones (Ziadi-Künzli and Tachihara 2016). Both males and females are highly territorial. Females establish territories of 10-15 meters diameter, where they forage, shelter and seek suitable spawning sites (Künzli and Tachihara 2012, Ziadi-Künzli and Tachihara 2016). Male territories encompass up to five female territories that they defend, suggesting a haremic mating system (Kuwamura 1997). These territories are maintained year round and are very stable. In Okinawa, Kuwamura (1997) observed that 75% of males and 82% of females maintained their territories for eight years. When any male or female is removed, they are usually replaced by other individuals or the neighbour extends its territory. Therefore, territory arrangement is stable, even if owners change (Kuwamura 1997, Ziadi-Künzli and Tachihara 2016).

In Okinawa, the breeding season extends from May to September (Kuwamura 1997, Künzli and Tachihara 2012). Spawning occurs during one week around the new or full moons, and females may spawn up to three times in each period (Kuwamura 1997, Ziadi-Künzli and Tachihara 2016). Females lay adhesive demersal eggs masses in their territories around sunrise, attaching them to sand, coral rubble, algae or rock (Kuwamura 1997, Ziadi-Künzli and Tachihara 2016). Females stay in the nest after spawning caring for the eggs by fanning them and attacking intruders, while males leave to forage or to visit other females. Without maternal care, eggs do not survive (Kuwamura 1997, Ziadi-Künzli and Tachihara 2016). After constant care, approximately 55,500 larvae hatch around sunset of the spawning day and become planktonic, settling at a minimum size of 2 cm SL (Kuwamura 1997, Künzli and Tachihara 2012). In Okinawa, newly recruited young of the year were observed in August and had grown to 8 cm by June (Künzli and Tachihara 2012). Males grow larger and faster than females, as they are generally larger than all the females in their harem, attaining a maximum standard length of 20.9 cm while females grow to 17.6 cm SL (Künzli and Tachihara 2012, Ziadi-Künzli and Tachihara 2016). In Okinawa, 50% of males reach maturity at 14.8 cm SL and females at 12 cm SL and 1.5 years of age (Künzli and Tachihara 2012, Ziadi-Künzli and Tachihara 2016). Males can live to 13.5 years and females to 9.5 years (Ziadi-Künzli and Tachihara 2016).
documentation.threats: There are no known major threats.
documentation.measures: There are no species-specific conservation measures.
documentation.use_trade: This species is a component of the aquarium trade (Rajasuriya 2013, Malsack 2017).
documentation.rationale: This widely distributed reef-associated species is common in parts of its range and can be locally abundant. There are no known major threats; therefore, it is listed as Least Concern.
